## Three-hour cardio recording from effort to rest

### Data import and preparation

We analyse a 3-hour-and-10-minute recording from an Aidlab chest strap (MIT
licence) to identify the exercise and recovery periods, and to compare linear,
mono-exponential and bi-exponential models of heart rate recovery.

We use the RR intervals as our main signal because they provide one heart rate
value per beat (about 16 700 values), whereas the device pulse signal provides
one value about every 5 s (2 456 values). This allows us to follow heart rate
changes in greater detail. Each RR interval is the time between two heartbeats
in milliseconds; we convert it into heart rate in beats per minute with
$HR = 60\,000 / RR$. The pulse signal is kept as an independent check.

We also use the acceleration to estimate movement, and the body position to
examine posture. All timestamps are converted into time since the start of the
recording, so that the signals can be compared.

To summarise movement, we compute the standard deviation of the acceleration
magnitude in 60-s windows. Section 04 uses 10-s windows for its much shorter
7-min-30-s recording; over three hours, longer windows make the overall
movement patterns easier to see, although they may hide very brief movements.

```{r}
#| label: r3h-import
library(tidyverse)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Location of the data and start time of the recording
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

# Folder where the unzipped files are stored
r3h_dir <- "data/cardio-recovery-3h10m"

# dataset.json contains the metadata (title, start/end time, signals...)
r3h_meta <- jsonlite::read_json(file.path(r3h_dir, "dataset.json"))

# Start of the recording, in Unix milliseconds.
# We use it as the time origin: every timestamp will be expressed
# relative to this moment.
r3h_t0 <- r3h_meta$from_timestamp_ms


# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Beat-to-beat heart rate from RR intervals (main signal)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

r3h_rr <- read_csv(file.path(r3h_dir, "rr.csv"),
                   show_col_types = FALSE) |>   # hide the column message
  mutate(
    # timestamp is in ms since 1970 -> subtract the start and
    # divide by 1000 to get seconds since the start of the recording
    t     = (timestamp - r3h_t0) / 1000,
    # same time in minutes (easier to read on 3-hour plots)
    t_min = t / 60,
    # "value" = time between two heartbeats, in milliseconds
    rr    = value,
    # heart rate in bpm: 60 000 ms in one minute / duration of one beat
    hr    = 60000 / rr
  )


# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Heart rate computed by the device ("pulse", ~1 value / 5 s)
#    -> used only as an independent check of the RR-based HR
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

r3h_pulse <- read_csv(file.path(r3h_dir, "pulse.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    t     = (timestamp - r3h_t0) / 1000,   # seconds from start
    t_min = t / 60,                        # minutes from start
    hr    = value                          # already in bpm
  )


# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Movement from the accelerometer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# The accelerometer gives x, y, z (in g) many times per second.
# 1) We combine the 3 axes into one magnitude: sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)
# 2) We compute its standard deviation (SD) in 60-s windows:
#    - SD close to 0  -> the person is still
#    - larger SD      -> the person is moving

r3h_acc <- read_csv(file.path(r3h_dir, "acceleration.csv"),
                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>   # big file: takes a few seconds
  mutate(
    t   = (timestamp - r3h_t0) / 1000,     # seconds from start
    mag = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)            # magnitude of acceleration
  ) |>
  # floor(t / 60) * 60 = start of the 60-s window the sample belongs to
  # + 30           = middle of the window (better for plotting)
  group_by(t = floor(t / 60) * 60 + 30) |>
  summarise(acc_sd = sd(mag),              # movement indicator per window
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(t_min = t / 60)                   # minutes from start


# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Body position (code + text label)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

r3h_pos <- read_csv(file.path(r3h_dir, "body-position.csv"),
                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(t     = (timestamp - r3h_t0) / 1000,
         t_min = t / 60)

# Look at the column names (we don't know them in advance)
names(r3h_pos)

# Count how many times each position code/label appears
# (across(-c(timestamp, t, t_min)) = all columns except the time ones)
r3h_pos |>
  count(across(-c(timestamp, t, t_min)))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Summary table: how many points and which time span per signal
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

tibble(
  signal      = c("RR intervals", "pulse", "acceleration (60-s windows)", "body position"),
  n           = c(nrow(r3h_rr), nrow(r3h_pulse), nrow(r3h_acc), nrow(r3h_pos)),
  t_start_min = c(min(r3h_rr$t_min), min(r3h_pulse$t_min), min(r3h_acc$t_min), min(r3h_pos$t_min)),
  t_end_min   = c(max(r3h_rr$t_min), max(r3h_pulse$t_min), max(r3h_acc$t_min), max(r3h_pos$t_min))
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Signals used in the analysis (3h10m recording)")
```

The four signals cover the whole recording (0 to 190 min, i.e. 3 h 10 min), so the data set is complete enough for the analysis. The 16 684 RR intervals over 190 min correspond to a mean heart rate of about 88 bpm, which is consistent with a heart rate falling from about 128 to 66 bpm, as described in the data set. The device pulse signal contains 2 456 values, i.e. about one value every 5 s, as expected. The acceleration was summarised into 190 windows of 60 s, i.e. one value per minute, which is enough to follow changes in physical activity over three hours. The body position signal is of limited use: 192 of the 206 samples are labelled `unknown`, and only 14 samples indicate a lying position (prone, supine or on one side).

### Signal quality

Before fitting the models, we check the quality of the RR intervals to identify
measurement errors that could affect the results. We first look for recording
gaps, i.e. moments when two consecutive beats are more than 3 s apart, which
means that the device stopped recording. We then look for artefacts, i.e. RR
intervals that differ by more than 20 % from the previous one, which usually
indicate a missed or an extra beat detection. Gaps are detected before removing
the artefacts, because removing beats would otherwise create artificial gaps.
Following the data set documentation, gaps are only located and are not filled
in; artefacts are removed.

```{r}
#| label: r3h-quality

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2a. Recording gaps
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Normally, two consecutive beats are less than 1-2 s apart.
# If the time between two beats is much longer (here > 3 s),
# the device stopped recording: this is a gap, not a real beat.
# The README says gaps are preserved and not filled in,
# so we only locate them; we do NOT fill them.

r3h_gaps <- r3h_rr |>
  mutate(dt = t - lag(t)) |>              # time since the previous beat (s)
  filter(dt > 3) |>                       # keep only abnormal intervals
  transmute(
    gap_start_min = (t - dt) / 60,        # last beat before the gap (min)
    gap_end_min   = t_min,                # first beat after the gap (min)
    duration_s    = dt                    # length of the gap (s)
  )

# Table of all gaps
r3h_gaps |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1,
               caption = "Recording gaps in the RR series (> 3 s between beats)")

# Overall summary of the gaps
r3h_gaps |>
  summarise(n_gaps         = n(),
            total_gap_min  = sum(duration_s) / 60,
            longest_gap_s  = if (n() == 0) 0 else max(duration_s)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Summary of recording gaps")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2b. RR artefacts (missed or extra beats)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# A common rule: an RR interval is an artefact if it differs by more
# than 20 % from the previous one (a real heart cannot change that
# fast from one beat to the next).

r3h_rr <- r3h_rr |>
  mutate(
    rel_change = abs(rr / lag(rr) - 1),   # relative change vs previous beat
    artefact   = !is.na(rel_change) &     # first beat has no previous one
                 rel_change > 0.20        # TRUE if change > 20 %
  )

# Quality table: before removing anything
r3h_rr |>
  summarise(n_beats     = n(),
            n_artefacts = sum(artefact),
            pct_artefacts = 100 * mean(artefact),
            rr_min_ms   = min(rr),  rr_max_ms  = max(rr),
            hr_min_bpm  = min(hr),  hr_max_bpm = max(hr)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "RR interval quality check")

# Remove the artefacts: from now on, r3h_rr only contains clean beats
r3h_rr <- filter(r3h_rr, !artefact)

summary(r3h_rr$hr)
```

No recording gap longer than 3 s was found in the RR series. The gaps reported in `dataset.json` (up to about 60 s) concern the raw ECG, respiration and acceleration signals, not the RR intervals, which cover the whole recording.

Using the 20 % rule, 71 of the 16 684 RR intervals (0.4 %) were identified as artefacts and removed. This very low proportion shows that the RR series is of good quality. After cleaning, heart rate ranges from about 52 to 158 bpm (median 89 bpm), which is physiologically plausible. The maximum is higher than the 128 bpm mentioned in the data set description, which suggests that a period of higher effort occurs during the recording; this is examined in the next section.

### Identifying the exercise and recovery periods

The data set does not provide any activity labels, so we used the acceleration
signal to estimate when the participant was exercising and when they were
recovering.

**Exercise bouts.** We define an exercise bout as a period of increased
movement. A minute is considered active when the standard deviation (SD) of the
acceleration magnitude exceeds 0.1 g. We chose this threshold by inspecting the
movement signal: the SD is very low during most of the recording (median
0.013 g; 75 % of the minutes below 0.035 g), whereas only 8 minutes exceed
0.1 g, with values from 0.10 to 0.71 g. A threshold of 0.1 g therefore separates
these movement peaks from the rest of the recording. A higher threshold would
miss part of the activity: with 0.2 g, the third bout (0.197 g at 54.5 min) would
not be detected at all. This threshold is an estimate: an active minute does
not guarantee that the participant was exercising, and exercise with little
trunk movement may not be detected.

**Grouping active minutes.** Active minutes separated by no more than 3 min are
grouped into the same bout. This allows short breaks within an exercise period
without treating them as separate activities; for example, the two close
movement peaks around 25 and 28 min form a single bout. The time between the end
of a bout and the start of the next one is considered a recovery period.

**Figure details.** Because there are many heart rate values per minute, we
also compute the mean heart rate for each minute (red line) to make the overall
trend easier to see. Each mean is plotted at the middle of its one-minute
window: for example, the beats recorded between 10 and 11 min are plotted at
10.5 min. The same convention is used for the 60-s acceleration windows. Finally,
most body-position samples are labelled `unknown`, so we only plot the samples
with a known lying position; they appear as small blue vertical marks at the top
of the heart rate panel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-r3h-overview
#| fig-cap: "3h10m recording. Grey areas: exercise bouts (acceleration SD > 0.1 g). Blue areas: recovery periods following each bout. Top: beat-to-beat HR from RR intervals (grey points), device pulse (black) and 1-min mean HR (red); lying positions are marked at the top (blue ticks). Bottom: movement (SD of acceleration magnitude, 60-s windows); dashed line = 0.1 g threshold."
#| fig-height: 6

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3a. Detect the exercise bouts from the movement signal
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_acc_threshold <- 0.1   # g: above this, the minute is considered "active"

r3h_bouts <- r3h_acc |>
  filter(acc_sd > r3h_acc_threshold) |>          # keep only active minutes
  # Active minutes less than 3 min apart belong to the same bout
  # (so the two close peaks around 25 and 28 min form one bout)
  mutate(bout = cumsum(t_min - lag(t_min, default = -Inf) > 3)) |>
  group_by(bout) |>
  summarise(start_min = min(t_min) - 0.5,         # beginning of the first active minute
            end_min   = max(t_min) + 0.5,         # end of the last active minute
            .groups = "drop")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3b. Recovery periods = from the end of a bout to the start of the next one
#     (the last recovery lasts until the end of the recording)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_recoveries <- r3h_bouts |>
  transmute(bout,
            start_min = end_min,
            end_min   = lead(r3h_bouts$start_min, default = max(r3h_rr$t_min)))

# Show both tables
knitr::kable(r3h_bouts, digits = 1, caption = "Exercise bouts detected from movement")
knitr::kable(r3h_recoveries, digits = 1, caption = "Recovery periods following each bout")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3c. Mean heart rate per minute + lying positions (as before)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_hr_1min <- r3h_rr |>
  group_by(t_min = floor(t_min) + 0.5) |>
  summarise(hr = mean(hr), .groups = "drop")

r3h_lying <- r3h_pos |>
  filter(position != "unknown")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3d. Shaded areas, added to both panels
#     (drawn first, so the data appear on top of them)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_shading <- list(
  geom_rect(data = r3h_recoveries, inherit.aes = FALSE,
            aes(xmin = start_min, xmax = end_min, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25),
  geom_rect(data = r3h_bouts, inherit.aes = FALSE,
            aes(xmin = start_min, xmax = end_min, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            fill = "grey40", alpha = 0.30)
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3e. Top panel: heart rate
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_p1 <- ggplot() +
  r3h_shading +
  geom_point(data = r3h_rr, aes(t_min, hr), colour = "grey70", size = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = r3h_pulse, aes(t_min, hr), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = r3h_hr_1min, aes(t_min, hr), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_rug(data = r3h_lying, aes(x = t_min), sides = "t", colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 190, by = 10)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Heart rate (bpm)") +
  theme_minimal()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3f. Bottom panel: movement, with the threshold line
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_p2 <- ggplot(r3h_acc, aes(t_min, acc_sd)) +
  r3h_shading +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = r3h_acc_threshold, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 190, by = 10)) +
  labs(x = "Time from start of recording (min)", y = "Acceleration SD (g)") +
  theme_minimal()

patchwork::wrap_plots(r3h_p1, r3h_p2, ncol = 1, heights = c(2, 1))
```

What we observe:

- **Three exercise bouts** were detected: 10–13 min, 24–29 min (two close peaks) and 54–55 min. Each bout is followed by an increase in heart rate.
- **0–10 min:** heart rate is already high (125–140 bpm), although movement stays below the threshold. The participant was probably exercising with little trunk movement, which a
chest accelerometer does not detect well. We therefore consider that the first bout covers 0–13 min.
- **Recovery 1 (13–24 min):** heart rate falls steadily from about 135 to 105 bpm, with little movement.
- **Recovery 2 (29–54 min):** heart rate falls to about 100 bpm and then stays on a plateau, while light movement continues. This is an active recovery.
- **Recovery 3 (55–190 min):** after the last bout, movement almost stops and heart rate decreases slowly from about 115 to 65 bpm over more than two hours, with short isolated peaks (possibly changes in body position).
- The body position signal is mostly `unknown`; lying positions appear only sporadically and do not help to define the phases.

For each recovery period, $t = 0$ is the end of the preceding exercise bout.

### Fitting the models

We fitted three models to each recovery period separately, because each period
has a different heart rate pattern:

- **Linear:** $HR(t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t$
- **Mono-exponential:** $HR(t) = HR_\infty + a\,e^{-t/\tau}$
- **Bi-exponential:** $HR(t) = HR_\infty + a_1 e^{-t/\tau_1} + a_2 e^{-t/\tau_2}$

where $HR_\infty$ is the plateau, $a$, $a_1$, $a_2$ the amplitudes of the
decrease and $\tau$, $\tau_1$, $\tau_2$ the time constants. For each period,
time is reset to zero at the end of the preceding exercise bout, so that $t$
measures the time since the start of recovery.

The linear model was fitted with `lm()` and the exponential models by
non-linear least squares with `nls()`. Non-linear models need starting values:
we used the mean heart rate during the first 30 s to estimate the initial heart
rate and the median heart rate during the last 20 % of the period to estimate
the plateau; their difference gives an initial estimate of the amplitude. We
constrained amplitudes to be positive and time constants to be at least 1 s.

The bi-exponential model has five parameters and is harder to fit. We therefore
tried three sets of starting values (the first one based on the time constants
reported by @joseph2023) and kept the converged fit with the smallest residual
sum of squares, i.e. the smallest overall difference between predicted and
measured heart rates.

For each parameter, we report an approximate 95 % confidence interval
(estimate ± 1.96 × standard error). These intervals are only approximate for
non-linear models, and they are probably too narrow here because the
beat-to-beat residuals are autocorrelated (see the model comparison).

```{r}
#| label: r3h-fit

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4a. Extract one recovery period and reset time to 0
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# start_min / end_min come from the r3h_recoveries table (step 3).
# t becomes the time (s) since the END of the preceding exercise bout.
r3h_get_recovery <- function(start_min, end_min) {
  r3h_rr |>
    filter(t_min >= start_min, t_min <= end_min) |>   # keep this period only
    mutate(t = t - start_min * 60) |>                  # t = 0 at end of exercise
    select(t, hr)
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4b. Fit the 3 models to one recovery period
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_fit_models <- function(d) {

  # Starting values estimated from the data themselves:
  hr_start <- mean(d$hr[d$t < 30])                    # mean HR in the first 30 s
  hr_end   <- median(d$hr[d$t > 0.8 * max(d$t)])      # median HR in the last 20 %
  amp      <- max(hr_start - hr_end, 1)               # size of the HR drop (bpm)

  # --- Linear model: HR = b0 + b1 * t
  linear <- lm(hr ~ t, data = d)

  # --- Mono-exponential: HR = hr_inf + a * exp(-t / tau)
  #     hr_inf = plateau, a = amplitude, tau = time constant (s)
  #     "port" algorithm allows bounds (a >= 0, tau >= 1 s)
  mono <- tryCatch(
    nls(hr ~ hr_inf + a * exp(-t / tau), data = d,
        start = list(hr_inf = hr_end, a = amp, tau = 60),
        algorithm = "port",
        lower = c(0, 0, 1), upper = c(200, 200, 1e5),
        control = list(maxiter = 500)),
    error = function(e) NULL)                          # NULL if it fails

  # --- Bi-exponential: HR = hr_inf + a1*exp(-t/tau1) + a2*exp(-t/tau2)
  #     Very sensitive to starting values -> we try several
  #     (first one inspired by Joseph et al. 2023: tau1 ~ 44 s, tau2 ~ 120 s)
  starts <- list(
    list(hr_inf = hr_end,      a1 = 0.6 * amp, tau1 = 40, a2 = 0.4 * amp, tau2 = 120),
    list(hr_inf = hr_end,      a1 = 0.5 * amp, tau1 = 60, a2 = 0.5 * amp, tau2 = 600),
    list(hr_inf = hr_end - 10, a1 = 0.5 * amp, tau1 = 60, a2 = 0.5 * amp, tau2 = 3000)
  )
  bi_fits <- map(starts, \(s) tryCatch(
    nls(hr ~ hr_inf + a1 * exp(-t / tau1) + a2 * exp(-t / tau2), data = d,
        start = s, algorithm = "port",
        lower = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 1), upper = c(200, 200, 1e4, 200, 1e5),
        control = list(maxiter = 500)),
    error = function(e) NULL))
  bi_fits <- compact(bi_fits)                          # remove failed fits
  # keep the fit with the smallest residual sum of squares (deviance)
  bi <- if (length(bi_fits) == 0) NULL else bi_fits[[which.min(map_dbl(bi_fits, deviance))]]

  list(linear = linear, mono = mono, bi = bi)
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4c. Apply to the 3 recovery periods
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# One row per recovery; "data" and "models" are list-columns
r3h_rec <- r3h_recoveries |>
  mutate(
    label  = paste0("Recovery ", bout, " (", start_min, "–", round(end_min), " min)"),
    data   = map2(start_min, end_min, r3h_get_recovery),   # the beats of each period
    models = map(data, r3h_fit_models)                     # the 3 fitted models
  )

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4d. Table of fitted parameters (estimate + standard error + 95 % CI)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_param_table <- function(m, model_name) {
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)                         # skip failed fits
  s <- summary(m)$coefficients
  tibble(model     = model_name,
         parameter = rownames(s),
         estimate  = s[, 1],
         SE        = s[, 2],
         CI_low    = s[, 1] - 1.96 * s[, 2],
         CI_high   = s[, 1] + 1.96 * s[, 2])
}

r3h_rec |>
  mutate(params = map(models, \(ms) imap(compact(ms), r3h_param_table) |> list_rbind())) |>
  select(label, params) |>
  unnest(params) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Fitted parameters for each recovery period (time in s)")
```

```{r}
#| label: r3h-plot-function

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Predicted curves and observed data (same as before)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_pred <- r3h_rec |>
  mutate(pred = map2(data, models, \(d, ms) {
    grid <- tibble(t = seq(0, max(d$t), length.out = 500))
    imap(compact(ms), \(m, name)
         mutate(grid, model = name, hr = predict(m, newdata = grid))) |>
      list_rbind()
  })) |>
  select(bout, pred) |>
  unnest(pred)

r3h_obs <- r3h_rec |>
  select(bout, data) |>
  unnest(data)

r3h_model_colours <- c(linear = "#1b9e77", mono = "#7570b3", bi = "#d95f02")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Function: plot one recovery period
#   i       = number of the recovery (1, 2 or 3)
#   max_min = optional: only show the first max_min minutes (zoom)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_plot_recovery <- function(i, max_min = Inf) {
  rec <- r3h_rec[r3h_rec$bout == i, ]                       # info on this recovery
  obs <- filter(r3h_obs,  bout == i, t <= max_min * 60)     # its data
  prd <- filter(r3h_pred, bout == i, t <= max_min * 60)     # its fitted curves

  ggplot(obs, aes(t / 60, hr)) +
    geom_point(colour = "grey60", size = 0.6, alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_line(data = prd, aes(colour = model), linewidth = 1.1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = r3h_model_colours,
                        breaks = c("linear", "mono", "bi"),
                        labels = c("Linear", "Mono-exponential", "Bi-exponential")) +
    labs(title = paste0("Recovery ", i, " (",
                        rec$start_min, "–", round(rec$end_min), " min of the recording)",
                        # add ": first 20 min" only when we zoom
                        if (is.finite(max_min)) paste0(": first ", max_min, " min") else ""),
         x = "Time since end of exercise (min)", y = "Heart rate (bpm)",
         colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-r3h-rec1
#| fig-cap: "Recovery 1 (after the first exercise bout): linear, mono- and bi-exponential fits. The bi-exponential model did not converge."
#| fig-height: 4

r3h_plot_recovery(1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-r3h-rec2
#| fig-cap: "Recovery 2 (active recovery after the second exercise bout): linear, mono- and bi-exponential fits."
#| fig-height: 4

r3h_plot_recovery(2)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-r3h-rec3
#| fig-cap: "Recovery 3 (after the last exercise bout, until the end of the recording): linear, mono- and bi-exponential fits."
#| fig-height: 4

r3h_plot_recovery(3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-r3h-rec3-zoom
#| fig-cap: "Zoom on the first 20 min of recovery 3."
#| fig-height: 4

r3h_plot_recovery(3, max_min = 20)
```

**Recovery 1 (13–24 min, @fig-r3h-rec1).** The mono-exponential model gives a time constant $\tau \approx 91$ s (95 % CI: 82–99 s), an amplitude of about 27 bpm and a plateau of about 106 bpm. These parameters are precise and physiologically plausible. The linear model misses the fast decrease at the beginning of recovery. The bi-exponential model did not converge, which suggests that the data do not contain enough information to estimate two distinct time constants over this short period.

**Recovery 2 (29–54 min, @fig-r3h-rec2).** The decrease in heart rate is small (amplitude of about 11 bpm) and heart rate quickly stabilises around 99 bpm, consistent with the light movement that continues during this period (active recovery). The mono-exponential time constant ($\tau \approx 86$ s) is estimated with a wide confidence interval (58–115 s). The bi-exponential model converged but is not interpretable: its second time constant is shorter than the first one and the confidence interval of its amplitude includes negative values. The two exponential components cannot be separated.

**Recovery 3 (55–190 min, @fig-r3h-rec3 and @fig-r3h-rec3-zoom).** This is the longest and calmest recovery period. Two processes are visible: a fast decrease in heart rate during the first minutes, then a very slow decrease over more than two hours.

- The mono-exponential model only captures the slow decrease ($\tau \approx 4\,570$ s, i.e. about 76 min, plateau ≈ 64 bpm). It misses the fast initial drop: its curve starts at about 97 bpm, whereas the observed heart rate is about 112 bpm (@fig-r3h-rec3-zoom).
- The bi-exponential model follows both phases. Its fast component ($\tau_1 \approx 174$ s, i.e. about 3 min; amplitude ≈ 21 bpm) describes the early recovery. However, its slow component is not physiologically interpretable: $\tau_2 \approx 16\,400$ s (about 4.5 h, longer than the recording itself) and the plateau ($HR_\infty \approx 31$ bpm) is far below any plausible resting heart rate. When $\tau_2$ is much longer than the observation window, $a_2 e^{-t/\tau_2}$ behaves like a straight line: the "slow phase" is in fact a linear drift of about 0.2 bpm/min. The same behaviour was observed on the 7.5-min recording.

The time constants of the fast phase (91 s for recovery 1, 174 s for recovery 3) are of the same order of magnitude as those reported in the literature, although longer than the 44–65 s found by @joseph2023 after a maximal test with supine recovery. The intensity of exercise in our recording is unknown, and recovery took place without controlled posture, which may explain part of this difference. The models are compared quantitatively in the next section.


### Model comparison and residual analysis

```{r}
#| label: r3h-compare

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5a. Fourth model: mono-exponential + linear drift
#     HR = hr0 + a * exp(-t / tau) + b * t
#     (same test as in the 7.5-min analysis)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_fit_drift <- function(d) {
  hr_start <- mean(d$hr[d$t < 30])
  hr_end   <- median(d$hr[d$t > 0.8 * max(d$t)])
  amp      <- max(hr_start - hr_end, 1)

  # try several starting values for tau, keep the best converged fit
  fits <- map(c(60, 120, 300), \(tau0) tryCatch(
    nls(hr ~ hr0 + a * exp(-t / tau) + b * t, data = d,
        start = list(hr0 = hr_end, a = amp, tau = tau0, b = 0),
        control = list(maxiter = 500)),
    error = function(e) NULL))
  fits <- compact(fits)
  if (length(fits) == 0) NULL else fits[[which.min(map_dbl(fits, deviance))]]
}

# Add this model to the list of models of each recovery
r3h_rec <- r3h_rec |>
  mutate(models = map2(models, data, \(ms, d)
                       c(ms, list(`mono + drift` = r3h_fit_drift(d)))))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5b. Indicators of goodness of fit and residual structure
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_indicators <- function(models, d) {
  imap(compact(models), \(m, name) {
    e <- resid(m)                                       # residuals
    tibble(
      model      = name,
      k          = length(coef(m)),                     # number of parameters
      RMSE       = sqrt(mean(e^2)),                     # typical error (bpm)
      R2         = 1 - sum(e^2) / sum((d$hr - mean(d$hr))^2),
      AIC        = AIC(m),                              # lower = better
      BIC        = BIC(m),                              # lower = better (penalises k more)
      DW         = sum(diff(e)^2) / sum(e^2),           # Durbin-Watson: 2 = independent
      acf_lag1   = acf(e, plot = FALSE)$acf[2],         # correlation with previous residual
      LjungBox_p = Box.test(e, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value
    )
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(dAIC = AIC - min(AIC), .after = AIC)         # difference with the best model
}

r3h_ind <- r3h_rec |>
  mutate(ind = map2(models, data, r3h_indicators)) |>
  select(label, ind) |>
  unnest(ind)

knitr::kable(r3h_ind, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 3),
             caption = "Model comparison for each recovery period")
```
```{r}
#| label: r3h-residuals-prep
# Nice names for the models (used as panel titles)
r3h_model_names <- c(linear = "Linear", mono = "Mono-exponential",
                     bi = "Bi-exponential", `mono + drift` = "Mono-exp. + drift")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5c. Residuals of every model, for every recovery
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_res <- r3h_rec |>
  mutate(res = map2(models, data, \(ms, d)
                    imap(compact(ms), \(m, name)
                         tibble(model = name, t = d$t, resid = resid(m))) |>
                      list_rbind())) |>
  select(bout, label, res) |>
  unnest(res) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("linear", "mono", "bi", "mono + drift")))

# Colours: same as the fit figures + one for the 4th model
r3h_model_colours4 <- c(r3h_model_colours, `mono + drift` = "#e7298a")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Function: by how much is the model above (+) or below (-) the real HR?
#   One small panel per model, values averaged in bins of bin_s seconds
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_plot_sign <- function(i, bin_s = 20, max_min = Inf) {
  d <- r3h_res |>
    filter(bout == i, t <= max_min * 60) |>
    # mean residual in each time bin (removes beat-to-beat noise)
    group_by(model, t = floor(t / bin_s) * bin_s + bin_s / 2) |>
    summarise(resid = mean(resid), .groups = "drop") |>
    # residual = real HR - model, so model - real HR = -residual
    #   e.g. model 10 bpm above the real HR -> +10
    mutate(error    = -resid,
           position = if_else(error > 0, "Model above real HR", "Model below real HR"))

  ggplot(d, aes(t / 60, error, fill = position)) +
    geom_col(width = bin_s / 60) +                     # one bar per time bin
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1, labeller = as_labeller(r3h_model_names)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Model above real HR" = "firebrick",
                                 "Model below real HR" = "steelblue")) +
    labs(x = "Time since end of exercise (min)",
         y = "Model − real HR (bpm)", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Function: HR + fitted models (top) and sign panels (bottom)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_plot_fit_sign <- function(i, bin_s = 20, max_min = Inf) {
  top    <- r3h_plot_recovery(i, max_min) + labs(x = NULL)
  bottom <- r3h_plot_sign(i, bin_s, max_min)
  patchwork::wrap_plots(top, bottom, ncol = 1, heights = c(1.5, 3))   # bottom = 2x taller
}
```

#| fig-height: 10

r3h_plot_fit_sign(1, bin_s = 20)

```{r}
#| label: r3h-summary

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5e. Final summary: how far is each model from the real HR, on average?
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_summary <- r3h_res |>
  mutate(model = as.character(model)) |>
  group_by(bout, label, model) |>
  summarise(
    mean_error = mean(-resid),          # signed mean (≈ 0: errors cancel out)
    MAE        = mean(abs(resid)),      # mean absolute error (bpm)
    RMSE       = sqrt(mean(resid^2)),   # penalises large errors more
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # add the number of parameters and ΔAIC from the comparison table
  left_join(select(r3h_ind, label, model, k, dAIC), by = c("label", "model")) |>
  # best model of each recovery = lowest AIC (ΔAIC = 0)
  mutate(best = if_else(dAIC == 0, "best (AIC)", ""),
         model = factor(model, levels = c("linear", "mono", "bi", "mono + drift"))) |>
  arrange(bout, model)

r3h_summary |>
  select(label, model, k, mean_error, MAE, RMSE, dAIC, best) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("Recovery", "Model", "Parameters", "Mean error (bpm)",
                             "MAE (bpm)", "RMSE (bpm)", "ΔAIC", ""),
               caption = "Summary of model performance for each recovery period")
```
```{r}
#| label: fig-r3h-summary
#| fig-cap: "Mean absolute error (MAE) of each model for each recovery period. The best model according to AIC is marked with a star."
#| fig-height: 4

ggplot(r3h_summary, aes(model, MAE, fill = model)) +
  geom_col() +
  # star above the best model (lowest AIC)
  geom_text(data = filter(r3h_summary, best != ""),
            aes(label = "best"), vjust = -0.3, size = 4) +
  facet_wrap(~label, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = r3h_model_colours4, labels = r3h_model_names) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = r3h_model_names) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +   # room for the star
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean absolute error (bpm)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

```

We compared the models using goodness-of-fit indicators (MAE, RMSE, $R^2$), the
Akaike and Bayesian information criteria (AIC, BIC), which penalise the number
of parameters, and the structure of the residuals over time (@fig-r3h-res1 to
@fig-r3h-res3-zoom). The signed mean error is zero for every model:
least-squares fitting balances positive and negative errors, so this value
cannot be used to compare models. We therefore used the mean absolute error
(MAE), i.e. the average distance between the model and the real heart rate.
The BIC gives the same ranking as the AIC for all recovery periods.

**Recovery 1 (13–24 min).** The linear model is clearly rejected
($\Delta AIC \approx 706$, $R^2 = 0.37$). Its residuals show a systematic
pattern: it underestimates heart rate by about 13 bpm at the start of recovery,
then overestimates it for several minutes (@fig-r3h-res1). The
mono-exponential model reduces the MAE from 4.9 to 3.4 bpm, increases $R^2$ to
0.65, and its errors alternate around zero. The mono-exponential + drift model
has the lowest AIC, but its improvement is negligible in practice (MAE 3.31 vs
3.35 bpm, same $R^2$). We therefore retain the mono-exponential model as the
most parsimonious and interpretable description of this recovery
($\tau \approx 91$ s). The bi-exponential model did not converge.

**Recovery 2 (29–54 min).** All models perform similarly (MAE 5.3–5.6 bpm) and
show the same residual pattern (@fig-r3h-res2). All models explain almost none
of the heart rate variation during this period ($R^2 \le 0.06$). The
mono-exponential model has the lowest AIC; the bi-exponential model, with two
extra parameters, does not improve the fit ($\Delta AIC \approx 2$, identical
MAE). The residual waves are not explained by any decay model: they follow the
changes in movement during this active recovery. The mono-exponential + drift
model did not converge.

**Recovery 3 (55–190 min).** The linear and mono-exponential models both miss
the fast decrease at the beginning of recovery: during the first 4 min, they
underestimate heart rate by up to 10–15 bpm (@fig-r3h-res3-zoom). The
bi-exponential and mono-exponential + drift models capture this fast phase and
give the same MAE (6.45 bpm) and nearly the same $R^2$ (0.485 and 0.484). The
bi-exponential model has the lowest AIC, but its slow component is not
physiologically interpretable ($\tau_2 \approx 4.5$ h,
$HR_\infty \approx 31$ bpm, see previous section). The mono-exponential + drift
model reaches the same accuracy with one parameter less, which confirms that
the "slow phase" of the bi-exponential model mainly describes a linear drift.

**Limits of the statistical comparison.** For all models and all recovery
periods, the residuals are strongly autocorrelated: the Durbin–Watson statistic
ranges from 0.10 to 0.17 (far below the value of 2 expected for independent
residuals), the lag-1 autocorrelation ranges from 0.91 to 0.95, and the
Ljung–Box test is highly significant ($p \approx 0$). Beat-to-beat heart rate
fluctuates with breathing and with changes in movement, which no smooth decay
curve can capture. With thousands of correlated beats, the AIC differences
overstate the evidence and should be read as indicative. The choice of model
must therefore also rely on residual structure, parsimony and physiological
interpretability.

**In summary**, the post-exercise decrease in heart rate is well described by a
mono-exponential decay with a time constant of about 1.5–3 min. On the long
recovery, this fast phase is followed by a slow, almost linear drift over
several hours, which reflects prolonged rest rather than a second exponential
recovery process.

### Sensitivity analyses

```{r}
#| label: r3h-sensitivity

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6a. Data sets to test
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_rec1 <- r3h_rec$data[[1]]                 # recovery 1 (RR), already prepared
r3h_rec3 <- r3h_rec$data[[3]]                 # recovery 3 (RR), already prepared
r3h_start3 <- r3h_rec$start_min[3]            # start of recovery 3 (min)

# Mean HR in 5-s bins (reduces beat-to-beat noise)
r3h_bin5 <- function(d) {
  d |>
    group_by(t = floor(t / 5) * 5 + 2.5) |>
    summarise(hr = mean(hr), .groups = "drop")
}

# Device pulse during recovery 3, with t = 0 at the end of exercise
r3h_pulse3 <- r3h_pulse |>
  filter(t_min >= r3h_start3) |>
  mutate(t = t - r3h_start3 * 60) |>
  select(t, hr)

# All the data sets we want to compare (t is in seconds)
r3h_sens <- list(
  "R3, first 5 min (RR)"        = filter(r3h_rec3, t <= 5 * 60),
  "R3, first 10 min (RR)"       = filter(r3h_rec3, t <= 10 * 60),
  "R3, first 20 min (RR)"       = filter(r3h_rec3, t <= 20 * 60),
  "R3, first 60 min (RR)"       = filter(r3h_rec3, t <= 60 * 60),
  "R3, whole (RR)"              = r3h_rec3,
  "R3, first 20 min (5-s bins)" = r3h_bin5(filter(r3h_rec3, t <= 20 * 60)),
  "R3, first 20 min (pulse)"    = filter(r3h_pulse3, t <= 20 * 60),
  "R1, whole (RR)"              = r3h_rec1,
  "R1, whole (5-s bins)"        = r3h_bin5(r3h_rec1),
  "R1, whole (5-s bins)"        = r3h_bin5(r3h_rec1),
  "R2, whole (RR)"              = r3h_rec$data[[2]],
  "R2, whole (5-s bins)"        = r3h_bin5(r3h_rec$data[[2]])
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6b. Fit the 3 models to one data set and keep the key results
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_sens_row <- function(d, name) {
  ms <- r3h_fit_models(d)                     # same function as in step 4

  # small helpers that return NA when a model did not converge
  get_coef <- function(m, p) if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else coef(m)[[p]]
  get_se   <- function(m, p) if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else summary(m)$coefficients[p, 2]
  get_aic  <- function(m)    if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else AIC(m)

  tibble(
    data          = name,
    n             = nrow(d),
    tau_mono      = get_coef(ms$mono, "tau"),                        # s
    tau_low       = tau_mono - 1.96 * get_se(ms$mono, "tau"),        # 95 % CI
    tau_high      = tau_mono + 1.96 * get_se(ms$mono, "tau"),
    hr_inf_mono   = get_coef(ms$mono, "hr_inf"),                     # plateau (bpm)
    tau1_bi       = get_coef(ms$bi, "tau1"),                         # fast (s)
    tau2_bi       = get_coef(ms$bi, "tau2"),                         # slow (s)
    dAIC_lin_mono = get_aic(ms$linear) - get_aic(ms$mono),           # > 0: mono better
    dAIC_mono_bi  = get_aic(ms$mono)   - get_aic(ms$bi)              # > 0: bi better
  )
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6c. Run on all data sets and show the table
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
r3h_sens_tab <- imap(r3h_sens, r3h_sens_row) |> list_rbind()

knitr::kable(r3h_sens_tab, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Data", "n", "τ mono (s)", "CI low", "CI high",
                           "HR∞ mono (bpm)", "τ1 bi (s)", "τ2 bi (s)",
                           "AIC linear − mono", "AIC mono − bi"),
             caption = "Sensitivity of the results to the time window and to the signal used")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-r3h-sensitivity
#| fig-cap: "Time constants estimated on recovery 3 for increasing window lengths (log scales). The mono-exponential τ increases with the window, whereas the fast bi-exponential τ1 stays around 3 min. The slow τ2 is always above the grey line, i.e. longer than the window itself. The 5-min window is not shown (no plateau could be estimated)."
#| fig-height: 5

# Recovery 3 windows fitted with RR intervals
r3h_win <- r3h_sens_tab |>
  filter(str_starts(data, "R3"), str_ends(data, "\\(RR\\)")) |>
  mutate(window_min = c(5, 10, 20, 60, round(max(r3h_rec3$t) / 60))) |>
  filter(window_min > 5)                       # 5 min: no plateau, not interpretable

# The 3 time constants in one long table
r3h_win_long <- bind_rows(
  r3h_win |> transmute(window_min, tau = tau_mono, low = tau_low, high = tau_high,
                       type = "Mono-exponential τ"),
  r3h_win |> transmute(window_min, tau = tau1_bi, low = NA, high = NA,
                       type = "Bi-exponential τ1 (fast)"),
  r3h_win |> transmute(window_min, tau = tau2_bi, low = NA, high = NA,
                       type = "Bi-exponential τ2 (slow)")
) |>
  filter(!is.na(tau))

r3h_tau_types <- c("Mono-exponential τ", "Bi-exponential τ1 (fast)", "Bi-exponential τ2 (slow)")

ggplot(r3h_win_long, aes(window_min, tau, colour = type, linetype = type)) +
  # grey dotted line: tau = window length
  geom_line(data = tibble(window_min = c(10, 135), tau = c(10, 135) * 60),
            aes(window_min, tau), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 40, y = 40 * 60 * 1.4, label = "τ = window length",
           colour = "grey50", angle = 18, size = 3.5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), width = 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 20, 60, 135)) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(60, 180, 600, 1800, 3600, 3 * 3600, 8 * 3600),
                labels = c("1 min", "3 min", "10 min", "30 min", "1 h", "3 h", "8 h")) +
  scale_colour_manual(breaks = r3h_tau_types,
                      values = c("#7570b3", "#d95f02", "#d95f02")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(breaks = r3h_tau_types,
                        values = c("solid", "solid", "dashed")) +
  labs(title = "Effect of the window length (recovery 3)",
       x = "Window analysed after the end of exercise (min)",
       y = "Time constant", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```
We first checked whether the results depend on the length of the window
analysed after the end of exercise (@fig-r3h-sensitivity). On recovery 3, the
mono-exponential time constant increases strongly with the window: from
174 s (about 3 min) over the first 10 min, to 330 s over 20 min, 549 s over
60 min and 4 572 s (about 1.3 h) over the whole recovery. The longer the window,
the more the mono-exponential model absorbs the slow drift of heart rate, so
its time constant no longer describes the post-exercise recovery itself. Over
the first 5 min only (not shown), the model cannot identify a plateau
($HR_\infty$ stuck at 0, confidence interval of $\tau$ including negative
values) and the linear model fits better: this window is too short.

In contrast, the fast time constant of the bi-exponential model is stable:
whenever the model converges, $\tau_1$ stays between 138 and 192 s, i.e. about
3 min, which matches the mono-exponential $\tau$ obtained over the first 10 min.
The slow time constant $\tau_2$ ranges from about 2.4 to 8 h and is always
above the grey line, i.e. longer than the window itself. It therefore never
describes a real exponential phase, only a slow linear drift. As a consequence,
the advantage of the bi-exponential model over the mono-exponential model grows
with the window length ($\Delta AIC$ from 29 over 20 min to 507 over the whole
recovery), because this drift accumulates over time.

```{r}
#| label: fig-r3h-sensitivity-signal
#| fig-cap: "Mono-exponential time constant τ (with 95 % CI) obtained with different signals."
#| fig-height: 3.5

r3h_sig <- r3h_sens_tab |>
  filter(data %in% c("R3, first 20 min (RR)", "R3, first 20 min (5-s bins)",
                     "R3, first 20 min (pulse)", "R1, whole (RR)", "R1, whole (5-s bins)",
                     "R2, whole (RR)", "R2, whole (5-s bins)")) |>
  mutate(recovery = case_when(str_starts(data, "R1") ~ "Recovery 1 (whole)",
                              str_starts(data, "R2") ~ "Recovery 2 (whole)",
                              str_starts(data, "R3") ~ "Recovery 3 (first 20 min)"),
         signal   = case_when(str_detect(data, "\\(RR\\)") ~ "RR intervals",
                              str_detect(data, "5-s bins") ~ "5-s bins",
                              str_detect(data, "pulse")    ~ "Device pulse"))

ggplot(r3h_sig, aes(tau_mono, signal)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = tau_low, xmax = tau_high),
                width = 0.2, colour = "#7570b3", orientation = "y") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#7570b3") +
  facet_wrap(~recovery, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Effect of the signal (mono-exponential τ)",
       x = "Time constant τ (s)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```
We then checked whether the results depend on the signal used
(@fig-r3h-sensitivity-signal): beat-to-beat heart rate from RR intervals, heart
rate averaged in 5-s bins, and, for recovery 3, the pulse signal computed by the
device. For each recovery, the mono-exponential time constant is similar
whatever the signal: about 91 s for recovery 1, about 86–93 s for recovery 2,
and 327–380 s over the first 20 min of recovery 3. The confidence intervals
overlap in all cases, so our estimates of $\tau$ do not depend on the signal.

The confidence intervals are, however, much narrower with RR intervals. This
does not mean that RR intervals give a more precise estimate: with more than
1 000 strongly autocorrelated beats, the standard errors assume many more
independent observations than there really are. The wider intervals obtained
with 5-s bins and pulse are probably more realistic. The same bias affects the
model comparison: over the first 20 min of recovery 3, the advantage of the
bi-exponential model is large with RR intervals ($\Delta AIC = 28.9$), but small
with 5-s bins (1.9) and pulse (6.1). On recovery 1, the bi-exponential model
fitted on 5-s bins collapses into the mono-exponential model
($\tau_1 = \tau_2 = 91$ s) and does not improve the fit.

Recovery 2 gives a time constant similar to recovery 1, but with a very wide
confidence interval, especially with 5-s bins (93 s, 95 % CI: 20–165 s). This is consistent with the
previous section: during this active recovery, heart rate barely decreases and
none of the decay models describes the data well ($R^2 \le 0.06$).

### Summary of findings for this recording

**Description of the recording.** The 3-hour recording does not contain a
single exercise followed by one recovery, but three exercise bouts (0–13,
24–29 and 54–55 min), each followed by a recovery period. Recovery 1
(13–24 min) is short and calm, recovery 2 (29–54 min) is active (light movement
continues), and recovery 3 (55–190 min) is long and passive.

**H1: the mono-exponential model describes recovery better than the linear
model. Supported.** On all three recovery periods, the mono-exponential model
has a much lower AIC than the linear model ($\Delta AIC$ between 140 and 693).
The linear model leaves a systematic pattern in the residuals: it
underestimates heart rate by 10–15 bpm at the start of recovery and
overestimates it later. It is also physiologically implausible, since it
predicts that heart rate keeps falling indefinitely.

**H2: after intense exercise and over a long period, the bi-exponential model
fits better, with a fast (≈ 40–60 s) and a slower (≈ 2 min) time constant
[@joseph2023]. Partly supported.** On the long recovery (recovery 3), heart rate
does show two processes: a fast decrease during the first minutes, then a very
slow decrease over more than two hours. The bi-exponential model has the lowest
AIC and its fast time constant is stable across windows ($\tau_1 \approx$
2.3–3.2 min). However, its slow component is not a second recovery phase: its
time constant (2.4 to 8 h) is always longer than the analysed window and its
plateau is physiologically impossible ($HR_\infty \approx 31$ bpm). A
mono-exponential model with a linear drift reaches the same accuracy with one
parameter less, and the advantage of the bi-exponential model almost disappears
when heart rate is averaged in 5-s bins. The second part of H2 is supported:
over the short recovery 1, the mono-exponential model is sufficient and the
bi-exponential model does not converge.

**H3: periods of continued movement deviate from the model, and the plateau is
higher than resting heart rate during active recovery. Supported.** During
recovery 2, heart rate stabilises around 99 bpm, far above the 65–70 bpm
reached at the end of the recording, and none of the decay models explains the
heart rate variations ($R^2 \le 0.06$). The residuals follow the changes in
movement. Recovery 1 also ends on a high plateau (about 106 bpm), because it is
interrupted by the next exercise bout.

**Chosen model.** We retain the **mono-exponential model**, fitted on a window
limited to the post-exercise recovery itself (about the first 10 min). It is the
most parsimonious model, its parameters are physiologically interpretable, and
its time constant is robust to the signal used. It gives
$\tau \approx 91$ s (about 1.5 min) after the first exercise bout and
$\tau \approx 174$ s (about 3 min) after the last one. These values are of the
same order of magnitude as those found on the 7.5-min recording
($\tau \approx$ 49–63 s) and in the literature ($\tau \approx 65$ s after a
maximal test, @joseph2023), but longer. When a long period after exercise is
analysed, a linear drift term must be added to describe the slow decrease of
heart rate, as in the 7.5-min recording. This drift is an empirical description,
not a recovery process.

**Limitations.**

- **Unknown protocol.** No activity labels are provided: the type and intensity
  of exercise are unknown. Exercise bouts were identified from a chest
  accelerometer, which does not detect well exercises with little trunk movement 
  (probably the case during the first 10 min). The end of each bout
  ($t = 0$) depends on an arbitrary threshold (0.1 g) and has a 1-min
  resolution.
- **Interrupted recoveries.** Recoveries 1 and 2 are interrupted by the next
  exercise bout, so heart rate never returns to rest. Only recovery 3 is long
  enough to study the full return to rest.
- **Uncontrolled conditions.** Posture, movement and breathing were not
  controlled, unlike in laboratory studies where participants recover lying
  down [@joseph2023]. This may explain our longer time constants.
- **Slow drift.** The slow decrease over several hours may reflect prolonged
  rest, sleep or circadian variations rather than recovery from exercise; the
  data do not allow us to tell these apart.
- **Autocorrelated residuals.** For all models, residuals are strongly
  autocorrelated (Durbin–Watson 0.10–0.17). AIC differences, standard errors
  and confidence intervals computed on beat-to-beat data overstate the
  evidence and should be read as indicative.
- **Single participant.** The results come from one recording of one person and
  cannot be generalised.
